newsitem.title: USA: US bank bill may cut bank direct securities powers.
newsitem.headline: US bank bill may cut bank direct securities powers.

text.p: A Congressional committee working on legislation to reform antiquated U.S. financial laws is considering paring back current rules that allow banks to deal directly in some securities, industry lobbyists said on Thursday.

But a spokesman for the House Commerce Committee said the panel is still gathering facts and no decisions have been made. "Everything is on the table," Mike Collins said. "We've made no decisions whatsoever."

Committee staff has held 40 meetings with interested parties, including banking, securities and consumer groups, Collins said. But the staff has not briefed committee members on the discussions and top members are busy with appropriations measures, Collins said.

Lobbyists said Commerce Committee staff expressed concerns that the Securities and Exchange Commission does not have sufficient authority over the limited bank securities dealing currently permitted, mainly involving U.S. government bonds and municipal general obligation debt.

SEC chairman Arthur Levitt last week urged the committee to close or limit loopholes in the legislation permitting banks to deal in so-called bank eligible securities. Bank regulators would have authority over such sales, but Levitt said SEC oversight was needed.

"An investor who purchases securities from a bank receives a different, and in our view, lower standard of protection than does an investor who buys securities from a registered broker-dealer," Levitt told the Commerce Committee in testimony on July 17.

The legislation before the committee, narrowly approved by the House Banking Committee last month, would tear down the 1933 Glass-Steagall Act's legal barriers prohibiting banks from engaging in other financial services.

Under the current bill, banks would be permitted to engage in a full range of securities underwriting activity subject to SEC oversight, but existing exceptions from SEC regulation for dealing in bank eligible securities and certain other transactions would be retained and enhanced.
"There is talk of eliminating some of the 16 exemptions for banks," said Larry LaRocco, the American Bankers Association's top lobbyist on securities issues.

In addition to the exception for bank eligible securities, banks would be able to transact for trust and custodial accounts, deal in private placements and engage in some other activities without SEC oversight. The Commerce Committee is not expected to curb all of those exceptions, lobbyists said.
The committee could eliminate some exceptions outright or limit such dealings to transactions with sophisticated institutions, one industry lobbyist said.

Alternatively, the committee could require larger banks, which already have SEC-regulated securities affiliates, to conduct all securities activity in their affiliates, while allowing smaller banks to continue dealing in eligible securities directly, the lobbyist said.
A provision in the Banking Committee bill to expand the list of bank eligible securities by adding municipal revenue bonds is likely to be eliminated, ABA's LaRocco said.
"That is in the crosshairs," he said. "It's a target."
The Banking Committee last month rejected an amendment from Rep. Ken Bentsen, Democrat of Texas, subjecting banks dealing in eligible securities to broker-dealer regulations.

The Commerce Committee is also expected to enhance the regulatory authority of state insurance regulators and scale back or eliminate a new national financial council, lobbyists said. But a committee staffer denied that the committee would scrap the Banking Committee's bill and start over from scratch.

The Commerce Committee has until mid-September to finish its work on the bill. The bill's ultimate fate remains murky, however. Congress has worked without success for more than a decade to reform Glass-Steagall.
